title: Paucae Quaedam Sententiae Piam Interpretationem Desiderantes
author: Cassianus Ioannes
source: Translated by Claude from tmp801.tmp801.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.

passages.original: Unicuique nostrum duo cohærent angeli, id est, bonus et malus, ut liber Pastoris docet. — De hoc libro Pastoris ita scribit Hieronymus in Catalogo virorulu illustrium : Hermas cujus apostolus Paulus ad Romanos scribens meminit, asseritur auctor esse libri qui appellatur Pastor, et apud quasdam Græciæ Ecclesias etiam publice legitur. Revera utilis liber, multique de eo scriptorum veterum usurpaverunt testimonia ; sed apud Latinos ignotus est. Haec Hieronymus. Cæterum tanto ante Tertullianus in libro de Pudicitia, eam scripturam ab omni concilio Ecclesiarum inter apocrypha et falsa judicatam affirmat. et demini Gelasius papa in cap. Sancta Rom. distinct. 15, ut apocrypham repulit. Itaque quod de malo angelo liber ille Pastoris affirmat, falsum est, licet id scripserit etiam Origenes homil. 55 in Lucam, nisi forte figurate, mali angeli nomine, qui nobis cohaeret, fomes ipse intelligatur peccati, qui ex mali angeli suggestione traxit originem.
passages.english: "To each of us two angels are joined, that is, a good one and a bad one, as the book of the Shepherd teaches." — Of this book of the Shepherd Jerome writes as follows in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men: "Hermas, whom the apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans, is asserted to be the author of the book which is called the Shepherd, and among certain churches of Greece it is even read publicly. It is in fact a useful book, and many of the ancient writers have drawn testimonies from it; but among the Latins it is unknown." So Jerome. But long before, Tertullian in his book On Modesty affirms that this writing was judged by every council of the churches to be among the apocryphal and false [writings]; and finally Pope Gelasius, in the chapter Sancta Romana, distinction 15, rejected it as apocryphal. Therefore what that book of the Shepherd affirms about the bad angel is false, although Origen too wrote it in his 35th homily on Luke, unless perhaps, figuratively, by the name of the bad angel that is joined to us, the tinder of sin itself is to be understood, which took its origin from the suggestion of the bad angel.
passages.notes: Scanning errors read as intended: 'virorulu' as 'virorum', 'demini' as 'demum' (finally). The text has 'homil. 55 in Lucam'. Origen's homilies on Luke number 39, and the reference is probably to homily 35, so '55' may be a misprint. 'Fomes peccati' (the tinder of sin) is the technical theological term for concupiscence.

passages.original: Neque Innocentius jejunium sabbati apostolorum præcepto justitutum tradit, sed exempto, nempe quia apostoli cum Christus pateretur jejunarunt. Quartani tamen et sextam ferias jejunio deputatas ab apostolis sensit Augustinus : illa, quia tunc consilium iniere de occidendo Domino; hanc vero quia in ea mortuus est; sabbato autem, quia quievit ip sepulero post opus redemptionis, ut olim Dens. peracto creationis opificio.
passages.english: Nor does Innocent report that the Saturday fast was instituted by a precept of the apostles, but by [their] example, namely because the apostles fasted when Christ suffered. Augustine, however, held that Wednesday and Friday were assigned to fasting by the apostles: the former because on that day they formed the plan to kill the Lord; the latter because on it he died; and Saturday because he rested in the tomb after the work of redemption, as God once [rested] when the work of creation was completed.
passages.notes: Scanning errors read as intended: 'exempto' as 'exemplo', 'justitutum' as 'institutum', 'Quartani' as 'Quartam', 'ip sepulero' as 'in sepulcro', 'Dens' as 'Deus'. The sentence on Saturday is elliptical, and a verb such as 'he thought it [observed]' seems to be implied.

passages.original: alii propter humilitatem mortis Domini jejunare, sicut Romana et nonnullæ Occidentis Ecclesiæ, inter quas fuit Africana, a qua Mediolanum profecta mater Augustini, cum ibi non jejunantes sabbato reperisset, hujusmodi responsum ab Ambrosio accepit : Quando Romae sum, jejuno sabbato, quando hic sum, non jejuno, ut ibidem Augustinus et epstola 128 ad Januarium narrat. Et quidem non de sabbati, sed de quartas et sextae feriae per annum jejunio, tamquam per totam Ecclesiam recepto, et ab apostolis tradito, idem cum Augustino scribunt Clemens Alexandrinus lib. VII Stromatum, Epiphanius haeresi 75, Origenes hom. 10 in Levir., Damascenus lib. de Haeresibus, in Ærianis.
passages.english: others, because of the humility of the Lord's death, fast, like the Roman and some churches of the West, among which was the African [church]. Augustine's mother set out from it to Milan, and when she found people there not fasting on Saturday, she received from Ambrose a reply of this kind: "When I am in Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast," as Augustine relates in the same place and in letter 128 to Januarius. And indeed, not about the Saturday fast but about the fast of Wednesday and Friday throughout the year, as received throughout the whole Church and handed down by the apostles, the same thing is written, together with Augustine, by Clement of Alexandria in book VII of the Stromata, Epiphanius in heresy 75, Origen in homily 10 on Leviticus, and Damascene in his book On Heresies, under the Aerians.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing from 'some... would rather relax the fast to signify rest'. 'Levir.' is read as 'Levit.' (Leviticus), and 'quartas' as 'quartae'. The number of the letter to Januarius is given as in the text.

passages.original: sed incautos reprehendit, qui vanis quihusdam inventis philosophorum capiuntur potius quam ex ipsorum stercore aurum excernant, et Ægyptio- rum se superstitione contaminant potius quam ipsis tamquam injustis possessoribus vasa detrahant ad veri Dei cultum transferenda, quod faciendum ese docet Augustinus lib. ude Doctrina Christiana c. 4, cum ethnicorum libris vacatur : quo delectu ac dis- crimine qui usi non sunt, maiarum hæresum sege- tem ac pabulum habuere philosophiam, ut scribit, Tertullianus lib. de Praescriptionibus haereticorum, et lib. adversus Hermogenem.
passages.english: but he rebukes the incautious who are captivated by certain vain inventions of the philosophers rather than sifting gold out of their dung, and who defile themselves with the superstition of the Egyptians rather than taking from them, as unjust possessors, the vessels to be transferred to the worship of the true God. Augustine teaches that this must be done, in book [II] On Christian Doctrine, chapter 4[0], when one devotes oneself to the books of the pagans. Those who have not used this selection and discernment have had philosophy as the seedbed and fodder of evil heresies, as Tertullian writes in his book On the Prescription of Heretics and in his book Against Hermogenes.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence: Cassian does not condemn the study of eloquence or philosophy, but... Scanning errors read as intended: 'quihusdam' as 'quibusdam', 'ese' as 'esse', 'ude' as 'de', 'maiarum' as 'malarum'. The text has 'lib. de Doctrina Christiana c. 4' with no book number. The passage on the Egyptians' gold is at book II, chapter 40, so the bracketed book number and chapter digit are supplied and the reference may be truncated.
